sections.title: A rule you've been using without naming it
sections.content: Back in A1 you met the basic version of this rule with kérek/kérem: egy or no article in front of the object means the indefinite form (kérek), while a/az in front of it means the definite form (kérem). You've been living inside that rule ever since — Károly olvassa a könyvet ("Károly reads THE book"), hozom ("I'll bring it"), meglátogatom Károly szüleit — all definite, because the object was one specific, known thing. This lesson makes the rule explicit and complete, with eszik and iszik as the test case, because they're the two most irregular verbs it applies to.

items.english: I'm eating soup. (some soup, in general)
I'm eating the soup. (this particular soup, already on the table)
He/she is drinking the coffee. (the specific cup in front of them)

sections.content: Notice eszem does double duty — it's both "I eat [something]" and "I eat it [the specific thing]". Context tells you which: with no object at all, or an indefinite one, it's the general form; right after a/az plus a noun, it's the definite one. The clearest new forms to hold onto are eszi ("he/she eats it") and issza ("he/she drinks it") — the definite 3rd person is where the two conjugations look most different from each other.
